generated_summary: Cells must carefully control the amount of specific receptor proteins used by Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRLs) to ensure that the full variety of these molecular machines remains available for different tasks. If these levels become unbalanced, a few overabundant receptors can essentially hijack the core parts of the ligase, preventing other necessary receptors from working. When these receptor components are not regulated correctly, it can lead to many different diseases, including various types of cancer, particularly within the largest group of these ligases known as SCF ligases. One known way the cell manages the levels of these receptors, called F-box proteins, is by having the complete SCF complex trigger their own destruction through a process called ubiquitylation. In this study using yeast, researchers discovered a different pathway that breaks down an F-box protein called Met30 specifically when it is separated from its usual partner protein, Skp1. Surprisingly, this specific degradation process requires a core component called Cdc53/Cul1 but functions entirely without the help of the other major component, Skp1. The researchers proved that this unusual breakdown pathway is essential for maintaining the stability of chromosomes and for helping the cell defend itself against the stress caused by heavy metals. Most importantly, these findings reveal that a smaller sub-complex consisting of Cdc53, Rbx1, and Cdc34 has its own critical biological functions that do not depend on the presence of Skp1.
